# Italian musical terms — provenance report

<!-- Generated from authored/musical-terms.json by scripts/authored_decks.py. Do not edit: change the dossier and rebuild. -->

**Deck:** [`decks/musical-terms.ttl`](../decks/musical-terms.ttl) · **Cards:** 61 · **Licence:** [CC0 1.0 Universal](https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) · **Compiled by:** Anton Wiklund · **Created:** 2026-10-04

61 Italian terms from sheet music for tempo, dynamics, articulation and expression, from adagio and allegro to crescendo, staccato and dolce. The Italian term on the front, with its usual abbreviation where it has one; what it asks of the performer on the back, in English and Swedish, in our own words. Tempo terms describe a character, not a metronome figure. Checked against Theodore Baker's Dictionary of Musical Terms (1904), in the public domain, and Karl Gehrkens' Music Notation and Terminology (1914), in the public domain in the United States, with Wiktionary and Svensk ordbok.

## Licensing

The deck is CC0 1.0. Its two content sources are in the public domain: Baker's dictionary was published in 1895/1904 and its author died in 1934, so it is free both in the United States and under life + 70 years terms; Gehrkens' book was published in the United States in 1914 and is in the public domain there. Because Gehrkens died in 1975 his text may still be protected elsewhere, so from both books the deck takes only facts (what a term means, how it is abbreviated), which are not protected by copyright, and states them in its own words; no definition is copied, though a few short standard glosses (such as 'in a singing style', 'held for its full value') coincide with the books' wording. The selection of terms is the standard core vocabulary of performance directions, assembled for this deck from the topics both books cover, not copied from any list. Wikidata (CC0) was used only for machine checks of the Italian spelling. Wiktionary in English and Swedish (CC BY-SA 4.0; the English edition dual-licensed with the GFDL), Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Svensk ordbok (© Svenska Akademien) were consulted only to confirm meanings and Swedish usage: no selection was taken from any of them, and no wording beyond single ordinary words and common short phrases that any translation of the content sources would use (for example 'medelstarkt' for Gehrkens' 'medium loudly'). In review round 3 the backs whose wording followed Wiktionary more closely than the content sources (glissando, con brio, mezzo piano) were rewritten from Baker and Gehrkens. Their share-alike conditions and reserved rights therefore do not apply to the deck.

## Method

1. Choosing the content sources. Card content may only come from openly licensed or public-domain sources, so the meanings come from two public-domain reference works: Theodore Baker's A Dictionary of Musical Terms (G. Schirmer, 1904 printing of the 1895 work), whose OCR text was downloaded from the Internet Archive (item cu31924017810106, file cu31924017810106_djvu.txt, found with the archive.org advanced search API), and Karl W. Gehrkens' Music Notation and Terminology (1914), downloaded as plain text from Project Gutenberg (eBook #19499). Both were saved unchanged in the scratch directory. The exact commands are under Queries.
2. Choosing the terms. The deck editor's brief asked for about 60 Italian terms for tempo, dynamics, articulation and expression. A candidate list of 67 terms was drawn up from the terms both books treat as basic: Gehrkens' tempo groups (chapter XI, §109), his tempo changes (§§111–113), his dynamics list (chapter XIII, §§120–127), his signs and repeats (chapters IV–V) and his expression terms (§130), cross-checked with Baker's article Tempo-mark and his table of abbreviations. Six candidates were then left out for the reasons under Selection (andantino, ritenuto, fermata, stringendo, l'istesso tempo, con sordino), leaving 61. The selection is the standard core vocabulary of any music-theory course; it was not copied from a list in any one source.
3. Finding each term in the sources. For each term the Gehrkens text was searched for the paragraph that defines it (e.g. sed -n 2150,2870p for the tempo and dynamics chapters) and Baker's OCR text for its entry with a small script (baker_grep.py) that ignores the stress marks Baker prints inside headwords (Alle'gro). Baker's two-column OCR is noisy; where an entry was garbled (Allegretto, Mezzo piano, Brio) the card relies on the other sources and Baker's quoted text in the evidence is only what is legible. In the quotations from Baker below, his stress marks are left out, and obvious OCR misreadings of single letters in the quoted words are corrected (for example 'pid mosso' to 'più mosso', 'Zegatis'simo' to 'legatissimo', 's/acc.' to 'stacc.'); where a passage was too garbled to correct, it is not quoted.
4. Writing the cards. The front is the Italian term as both books spell it, with accents as in modern Italian (più, not piu). A frontNote gives the abbreviation where Baker's table of abbreviations or Gehrkens gives one that is in common use (cresc., dim., rit., pp, sfz, D.C., pizz., espr., Tempo I). The back is a short definition in our own words in English, and the same in Swedish, giving the character of tempo terms rather than a metronome figure, since both books stress that tempo words are relative (Gehrkens §108–109: "no absolute rate of speed can be indicated"; Baker, Tempo-mark: "They do not in themselves indicate a fixed and positive rate of speed, but only the general character of the movement"). A backNote adds the literal meaning or a short disambiguation where it helps (allegro 'cheerful', rubato 'robbed', decrescendo = diminuendo).
5. Cross-checking each card. Every card was checked against both public-domain books where both cover the term. Each card was also checked against the English Wiktionary entry where one exists, fetched with the Wiktionary REST API (https://en.wiktionary.org/api/rest_v1/page/definition/<term>), whose English and Italian sections were read for the musical sense; Wiktionary has no entry for tempo primo, meno mosso and più mosso, so those three rest on the two books alone (36 cards quote Wiktionary in their evidence). The Swedish wording was written by the authoring agent as idiomatic Swedish, translating the meaning given by the content sources. It was checked against Svensk ordbok (Svenska Akademien), queried through the search API behind svenska.se (https://svenska.se/api/search/so?q=<term>), for the 30 cards whose term has its own SO entry in the musical sense (mezzoforte was found in review round 1 under its one-word spelling; SO's dacapo is only the encore sense). In review round 1, 12 cards were checked against the Swedish Wiktionary (11 not covered by SO, plus mezzo forte, which has both) (and the three mezzo/fortepiano dynamics also against Swedish Wikipedia's article Dynamik (musik)). For the remaining 20 cards (larghetto, prestissimo, allargando, a tempo, tempo primo, meno mosso, più mosso, morendo, marcato, tenuto, arco, dal segno, attacca, grazioso, leggiero, tranquillo, sotto voce, pesante, giocoso, poco a poco) no Swedish reference with the term was found: their Swedish back is the authoring agent's translation of the English definition, not checked against a Swedish reference. Each card's evidence quotes what each source actually says, as seen on 2026-10-04.
6. Machine checks against Wikidata. One SPARQL query (under Queries) looked up every Wikidata item whose Italian label is one of the candidate terms, with its English and Swedish labels, descriptions and P31 classes; a few items were then read with wbgetentities. Where an item is clearly the musical term (by its description, its P31 'musical concept' Q115211517, 'dynamics' Q113558 or 'articulation' Q372923, or its sitelinks), the card has a check that the item's Italian label equals the front. 39 cards have such a check; the builder (authored_decks.py check/build) runs them against live Wikidata. Many common terms (piano, forte, dolce, fine, arco, grave, corona) have no musical item with that Italian label, only homonyms (plan, fort, sweetness, end, bow, falling body, crown), so those cards have no check. Wikidata descriptions were not used for content: several disagree with the reference works (see Quality control).
7. Who did the work. The research, the drafting and the cross-checking were done by AI agents (Claude, Anthropic) at Anton Wiklund's direction, with machine checks (the builder's dossier validation and Wikidata checks, and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and three independent AI review rounds (factual accuracy; language and translation; licensing, attribution and documentation), logged as rounds 1–3 under Quality control. The cards have not yet been reviewed by a human subject expert.

## Selection

Included: 61 Italian (or, for glissando, Italian-formed) performance directions that appear on the music itself and are part of the basic vocabulary every music-theory primer teaches: 12 tempo marks from grave to prestissimo, 9 changes of tempo (accelerando, ritardando, rallentando, allargando, a tempo, tempo primo, rubato, meno mosso, più mosso), 12 dynamic marks and changes (pianissimo to fortissimo, crescendo, decrescendo, diminuendo, sforzando, fortepiano, morendo), 8 terms for articulation and playing technique (staccato, legato, marcato, tenuto, pizzicato, arco, glissando, tutti), 4 road-map terms (da capo, dal segno, fine, attacca), 12 expression terms (dolce, cantabile, espressivo, grazioso, maestoso, agitato, con brio, leggiero, tranquillo, sotto voce, pesante, giocoso) and 4 modifiers that combine with all the others (molto, poco a poco, sempre, subito). Left out: andantino, because the sources disagree on whether it is faster or slower than andante (Gehrkens §109 notes it is 'now quite universally taken slightly faster than andante' although the word means 'less going'), so the card would have no single right answer; ritenuto, because whether it differs from ritardando (immediately slower rather than gradually) is contested (Gehrkens §111 says most composers do not distinguish them, Baker says it is 'often used incorrectly for rallentando'); fermata, because the card would not have one clean answer: Baker lists both Corona (It.) 'A hold' and Fermata (It.) with 'A hold' only as its second sense after 'a pause, stop, or interruption'; Gehrkens uses fermata as the English name of the sign; Wikidata Q830328 (the sign) has the Italian label 'corona'; and the Italian word fermata also means a stop; stringendo, l'istesso tempo and con sordino, to keep the deck near the brief's 60 cards with the most common terms. Also left out: names of forms and pieces (sonata, scherzo, toccata), voice types, instrument names, French and German terms, Latin terms (ad libitum) and metronome ranges, which vary between sources.

  VALUES ?it { "grave"@it "largo"@it "larghetto"@it "adagio"@it "lento"@it "andante"@it "moderato"@it "allegretto"@it "allegro"@it "vivace"@it "presto"@it "prestissimo"@it

    "pianissimo"@it "piano"@it "mezzo piano"@it "mezzo forte"@it "forte"@it "fortissimo"@it "crescendo"@it "decrescendo"@it "diminuendo"@it "sforzando"@it "fortepiano"@it "morendo"@it
    "staccato"@it "legato"@it "marcato"@it "tenuto"@it "corona"@it "fermata"@it "pizzicato"@it "arco"@it "glissando"@it "tutti"@it
    "da capo"@it "dal segno"@it "fine"@it "attacca"@it
    "dolce"@it "cantabile"@it "espressivo"@it "grazioso"@it "maestoso"@it "agitato"@it "con brio"@it "leggiero"@it "leggero"@it "tranquillo"@it "sotto voce"@it "pesante"@it "giocoso"@it
    "molto"@it "poco a poco"@it "sempre"@it "subito"@it }

## Quality control

7 rounds, 47 findings: 38 fixed, 1 rejected after checking, 8 needing no change. Every card's Wikidata checks (39 in all) are re-run against live Wikidata by `scripts/authored_decks.py check` before every build.

### Round 0: Source agreement, licence policy and Wikidata machine checks (2026-10-04)

**Reviewer:** Claude (AI) — authoring agent, machine checks · **Scope:** All 61 cards and the six candidates that were left out

Every card's meaning was confirmed in at least two sources, at least one of them a public-domain content source (Baker and/or Gehrkens), and in most cases also in Wiktionary or Svensk ordbok. The builder's Wikidata checks cover the Italian spelling of 39 fronts (the Italian label of the item for the musical term); they all pass. Wikidata's descriptions were compared with the reference works and not used, because several disagree with them. Terms on which the sources disagree were left out or given the convention in a note.

| Card | Issue | Resolution | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| andantino (left out) | Gehrkens §109: andantino 'is now quite universally taken slightly faster than andante' although by its form it means 'going less', i.e. more slowly; Baker's article Tempo-mark places it among the slow terms. The front would not have one right answer. | Left out of the deck. | fixed |
| ritenuto (left out) | Baker: 'Properly, held back, in slower tempo; but often used incorrectly for rallentando'. Gehrkens §111: some composers distinguish ritenuto (definitely slower) from ritardando (gradually slower), 'the majority of composers do not'. Contested. | Left out of the deck; ritardando and rallentando, on which the sources agree, are in. | fixed |
| fermata (left out) | The pause sign is called corona in Italian: Wikidata Q830328 (the musical symbol) has the Italian label 'corona' and no 'fermata'; the only Italian 'fermata' items are a bus stop (Q548662) and a legal term (Q106451578). Gehrkens and Baker use 'fermata' as the English name. A card with 'fermata' tagged as Italian would be wrong. [Corrected in round 3: Baker labels Fermata as Italian ("Fermata (It.) … 2. A hold") and also lists "Corona (It.) A hold"; only Gehrkens uses fermata as the English name. The exclusion stands: two Italian names and an ambiguous Italian word give no single clean answer.] | Left out of the deck. | fixed |

| rallentando | Is rallentando the same as ritardando?
